steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Shorehaven Lighthouse had stood on the ragged cape for generations, its white-washed tower braced against salt wind and the steady gnaw of waves. Its current keeper, Maeve Corrigan, was as much a fixture as the lantern room itself. Every evening she climbed the iron stairwell, wound the clockwork, and polished the Fresnel lens until it gleamed like a giant’s prism.  

The townspeople rarely saw her except on supply days, when she rowed across the narrow channel for kerosene, bread, and the occasional stack of library books. They said she had sea-glass eyes, that her hearing was so tuned to the water she could sense a storm hours before any barometer. They also whispered that she was searching for something—or someone—each night the beam swept across the shoals.

Maeve kept her own counsel. Her logbook was filled with tidy entries of wind speed and ship sightings, yet between the lines lived another story. Ten years earlier to the day, a schooner named The Northward Star had vanished in a gale not far from Shorehaven. On board was Callum Firth, the only person who had ever convinced Maeve to leave the lighthouse, if only in her imagination. They had planned a voyage: two weeks down the coast, warm harbors, charts spread across a teak table. The sea, however, cared little for plans.

Tonight, the anniversary, the air was oddly hushed—less like a lull than a deep breath drawn by the ocean. Gulls roosted early. The horizon dulled to pewter. Maeve trimmed the wick, adjusted the lens shutters, and waited. At 9:13 p.m. a distant rumble shuddered through the masonry, and a strange glow flickered in the mist.

She raised her spyglass. There, beyond the reef, bobbed a small vessel with a single reefed sail—a silhouette she knew the way one knows the line of their own hand. But the schooner in her glass was weather-stained, its paint scoured to bare planks, the name on its bow erased.

A rational keeper would have logged the sighting and signaled the coast guard. Instead, Maeve descended the stairs, heart hammering a rhythm the keepers’ manual never covered. She launched her dory, oars dipping silently, the lighthouse beam pivoting behind her like a blessing.

As she neared, the ghostly craft rocked gently, untethered. A scrap of sail slapped the mast. Maeve gripped the rail and peered into the cockpit. Rain-water pooled on warped boards; seaweed clung to cleats. No crew, no logbook, no lantern. Only a brass compass, curiously uncorroded, lay beside the helm. Its needle spun once, then settled—pointing not north, but straight at Maeve.

She lifted it. On the underside was a single etched word: Return.

Wind rose, snapping her collar. She looked toward the lighthouse: its lantern still burned, yet somehow dimmer, as though the very flame were holding its breath. In that faltering light Maeve made her choice. She took the compass, lashed her dory to the schooner, and trimmed the ancient sail.

The compass needle quivered, aligned. The schooner glided, answering a draft of wind that did not touch her face, as if moved by an older current. Behind her, the lighthouse flared brilliantly—one final sweep across the waves—then steadied back to its usual glow. Perhaps, Maeve thought, it was wishing her safe passage.

At dawn the townspeople found the dory adrift near the breakwater. The lighthouse lamp still revolved faithfully, wound as though its keeper had just climbed down for breakfast. In the logbook, the last entry was timed 9:12 p.m., neatly penned: Barometer falling. Lantern trimmed. All’s well.

Some afternoons, when fog lies low and the sea hushes its own voice, Shorehaven’s children claim they can hear another beacon out beyond the shoals—a faint, answering pulse that rises and fades like a heartbeat in the mist. The old sailors nod quietly. They set their courses by both lights now, the seen and the unseen, believing that somewhere past the horizon, Keeper Maeve keeps watch still, guiding wanderers home—even, perhaps, herself.
